components.text: Whether the Christian redemption account is better understood as truth or as consolation created to overcome suffering and meaninglessness.
Whether the stated redemption account is true or internally warranted, rather than merely consoling.
Whether Christianity merely supplies convenient consolation or offers a coherent explanation of suffering and a promised resolution.
Whether the religion's usefulness provides evidence that human beings created its story.
Whether Christianity's consolation is evidence that people created it to overcome suffering and meaninglessness.
Whether the asserted biblical worldview presents one morally and conceptually consistent God across its portrayals.
Whether divine love and saving grace cohere with jealous, vindictive, military, mutable, and localized portrayals.
Whether the same good God coherently creates, enters, judges, and ultimately restores a rebellion-damaged world.
Whether divine love and saving grace are consistent with the broader biblical portrayal of God.
Whether jealousy, anger, violence, mercy, and grace can consistently characterize the same God across both Testaments.
Whether jealousy, anger, violence, mercy, and grace can be reconciled across the two Testaments.
Whether the cited slavery permissions exhibit righteous opposition to evil or instead authorize ownership and unequal treatment.
Whether attributing injustice to human rebellion explains divine legislation permitting the purchase of people as property.
Whether divine love is morally compatible with legal permission to own foreign human beings.
Whether divine moral opposition to evil renders the cited slavery permissions righteous or consistent.
Whether human rebellion rather than divine approval explains unjust social institutions.
Whether Mosaic permission and regulation of slavery constitute divine moral endorsement of owning human beings.
Why the specific permission to purchase foreigners as property was necessary or humane.
Whether morally troubling Old Testament laws can be reconciled with divine goodness through accommodation to hardened hearts.
Whether permissive slavery legislation amounts to divine endorsement of ownership and unequal treatment.
Whether the regulation-as-accommodation defense explains a rule separating a freed man from his wife and children.
Whether a less coercive family-preserving rule was unavailable in the allegedly transitional legal setting.
Whether the slavery rules plausibly function as constrained regulation rather than morally avoidable authorization.
Why the specific family-separation rule was permitted rather than requiring the wife and children to leave with the freed man.
Whether the wider canon supplies moral principles opposed to human ownership and unequal dignity.
Whether broader biblical commitments to dignity and liberation create tension with coercive slavery rules.
Why the wife-and-children separation rule was necessary or compatible with a protective transitional purpose.
Whether broader biblical themes oppose treating people as slaves or unequal property.
Whether Galatians' statement that there is neither slave nor free establishes opposition to earthly slavery.
Whether the cumulative creation, Exodus, inclusion, and unity themes independently establish an anti-slavery canonical trajectory.
Whether Galatians' statement of unity independently entails abolition of earthly slave and free distinctions.
Whether one example of Priscilla teaching a man resolves an explicit instruction that women remain silent and subordinate in churches.
Whether the Priscilla episode and First Corinthians address the same institutional setting and kind of speech.
Whether one example of Priscilla teaching defeats an explicit Pauline restriction on women speaking in church.
Whether First Corinthians 14 imposes a universal prohibition on women's speech or addresses disorder in a particular congregation.
How the commands concerning subordination, husbands at home, and shame fit the proposed disorder-only interpretation.
Whether broader equality language abolishes earthly gender distinctions.
Whether First Corinthians 14 establishes a universal ban and subordination rule for women in church.
Whether male-female distinctions necessarily preserve parallel earthly restrictions despite spiritual equality.
